about: The roster of the Flagships tab of the Wine Atlas (codex58), wave one: 43 classic regions in 51 groups of five producers, each with the one flagship wine a sommelier is expected to know. A group is keyed by key, titled as the page heads it, tied to its region record (region, a slug of REGIONS.regions) and its country (country, the region's sheet key in REGIONS.countries), and written by its chunk. A pick is keyed by key (unique in the plan, the seed of the record's frozen id), names the producer as the house writes it, its WINE_PRODUCERS id where the library holds the house (producerId, empty when it does not), the flagship wine (the record's wine.name holds these words, and may add the Prädikat or the style the label prints), why a sommelier is expected to know it, and, where the spec agent was unsure, a note of what the author must confirm. An author may propose a swap only with a reason and the checker's agreement: it is recorded in the group's swaps (from, to, why, agreed) and the pick replaced in the same commit. schema.cjs holds every rule; build-flagships.cjs --plan proves this file against the app.

picks.why: Reims house of 1843: a multi vintage blend fermented in small old casks and built on a deep library of reserve wines, the house's own reason for being.
Épernay house of 1743; its vintage prestige cuvée, named for the Benedictine cellarer of Hautvillers, is the Champagne name a guest knows by heart.
picks.note: Teach Dom Pérignon as Moët & Chandon's prestige cuvée, made at Épernay; say how it is presented today only in words that do not age.

picks.why: Reims house of 1776; Cristal was made for Tsar Alexander II in 1876 and comes in clear glass with a flat bottom.
Aÿ family house of 1829, Pinot Noir led and partly fermented in old oak; La Grande Année is its vintage wine, aged under cork before disgorging.
Avize grower who fermented in barrel and kept a perpetual reserve; Substance, a Blanc de Blancs drawn from that reserve, made the grower movement's name. The one grower of the five.
Chablis family domaine of 1948 whose Grand Cru and Premier Cru wines, raised in old barrels, are cellared for decades.
Raveneau's kin in method: old barrels and long lives; Les Preuses is its Grand Cru on the slope's upper reaches.
picks.note: Confirm Les Preuses or Les Clos as the house's flagship and say why.

picks.wine: Chablis Grand Cru Bougros Côte Bouguerots
picks.why: A large holder of Grand Cru vines since 1959; Côte Bouguerots is the steep slope within Bougros.

picks.wine: Chablis Premier Cru Montée de Tonnerre
picks.why: The steel tank school of Chablis, with no oak since the 1960s; Montée de Tonnerre is its signature Premier Cru.
The cooperative of 1923; Château Grenouilles is its Grand Cru from Grenouilles, the smallest of the seven climats.
Vosne-Romanée domaine named in 1869 for its monopole, the vineyard the Prince de Conti bought in 1760.
Gevrey-Chambertin domaine built by Armand Rousseau from the early twentieth century, among the first in Burgundy to bottle its own wine.
Chambolle-Musigny domaine held by one family by descent since the fifteenth century; its Musigny comes from the larger part of the Grand Cru.
Chambolle-Musigny domaine of 1924; Bonnes-Mares from both the red and the white soils of the Chambolle side.
Morey-Saint-Denis Grand Cru monopole walled by Cistercian nuns, held by few owners since 1141.
Puligny-Montrachet family domaine and a biodynamic pioneer; Chevalier-Montrachet lies on the stony slope above Le Montrachet.
picks.note: Confirm Chevalier-Montrachet against Les Pucelles as the wine the house leads with.

picks.why: Meursault domaine founded by Jules Lafon in the 1890s; Les Perrières is the village's stoniest Premier Cru.
Meursault family domaine whose Corton-Charlemagne, made in very small quantity, is the rarest bottle a list may hold from it.

picks.wine: Volnay Premier Cru Clos des Ducs
picks.why: Volnay domaine whose Marquis fought fraud and championed estate bottling in the 1920s and 1930s; Clos des Ducs is its monopole.

picks.wine: Beaune Premier Cru Grèves Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus
picks.why: Beaune house of 1731; its monopole parcel in Grèves takes its name from the Carmelite nuns' devotion to the Infant Jesus.

groups.title: The Left Bank, the Médoc and Graves

picks.why: Pauillac, first of the first growths in the 1855 list; bought by Baron James de Rothschild in 1868.
Pauillac first growth by the Gironde, named for a fortified tower of the Hundred Years War; Les Forts de Latour is the second wine.
The first growth of the Margaux appellation, with a neoclassical château finished in 1815 and a white wine of its own, Pavillon Blanc.
Pessac-Léognan, the one Graves estate among the 1855 first growths, named in London by Samuel Pepys in 1663.
Pauillac, promoted to first growth in 1973, the one promotion in the 1855 list; an artist paints the label each vintage.

groups.title: The Right Bank, Saint-Émilion and Pomerol

picks.why: Pomerol Merlot on a button of blue clay, made famous after the Second World War by Madame Loubat and the Moueix family.
Pomerol's tiny estate of 1979, Merlot alone from a few rows, the first wine called a vin de garage.
Saint-Émilion estate on the Pomerol border, Cabernet Franc led on gravel and clay; the 1947 is a vintage of history.
Saint-Émilion côte estate on limestone named for the Roman poet Ausonius, Cabernet Franc led.
Saint-Émilion estate on gravel with an unusual share of Cabernet Sauvignon; promoted to Premier Grand Cru Classé A in 2022.
The one Premier Cru Supérieur of 1855, held by the Lur Saluces family from 1785 to 1999.
Barsac Premier Cru on red sand over limestone, Sémillon alone.
Barsac Premier Cru around a thirteenth century tower; its Cuvée Madame is made only in rare years.
Preignac Premier Cru beside Yquem, rich and Sémillon led, its gardens laid out in the seventeenth century manner.
Preignac estate that ages its Sauternes for many years in concrete vats before release, outside the 1855 list.
Ampuis house of 1946; La Mouline, first made in 1966, opened the single vineyard Côte-Rôtie of the three La La wines.
Tain house of 1834, its Hermitage named for the chapel on the hill; the 1961 is a vintage of history.
Mauves family in wine since 1481 by its own account; its Hermitage rouge blends parcels across the hill.
The Cornas family domaine that kept old vine, whole bunch Syrah alive in the appellation.
The family credited with keeping Condrieu alive when it was nearly abandoned; Coteau de Vernon is its oldest Viognier.
Courthézon estate of the Perrin family, all thirteen grapes planted, with an unusual share of Mourvèdre.
Sandy, north facing estate of old Grenache, a Châteauneuf of perfume rather than power.
Named for the Chappe telegraph tower on the plateau of La Crau, its rolled stones; the Brunier family since 1891.
Avril family estate whose single red blends parcels from across the appellation.
Gigondas estate with Roman era vats cut in the rock: the appellation beside Châteauneuf, under the Dentelles.

picks.why: Vouvray estate of 1928 whose three vineyards are made dry, medium dry or sweet as the year allows.

Romanèche-Thorins estate that ages Moulin-à-Vent in barrel, climat by climat, as Burgundy does.

picks.wine: Poggio all'Oro Brunello di Montalcino Riserva
picks.why: Estate of 1978 founded by an American importing family that took Brunello to a wide market abroad.
Estate of 1971 whose modern Brunello from the Tenuta Nuova vineyard drew new attention to the south east of the hill.

picks.why: The Incisa della Rocchetta family's Cabernet, first sold from the 1968 vintage; Bolgheri Sassicaia became a DOC of its own in 2013.

Suvereto estate of 1984 whose Merlot, Redigaffi, carried the coast's name south of Bolgheri.
